findings.title: Match statistics are written inside validation, so they get double-counted or rolled back
findings.body:
`BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves the row. It is called from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, so it runs on every validation pass. The counts end up wrong in two ways.

1. Double counting: `UsersController#create` always calls `user.valid?` (line 168; the `&&` evaluates `valid?` first) and then `user.save` (line 172), which validates again. Every signup attempt for a `do_nothing` email is counted twice.
2. Lost counts: `save`/`save!` run validations inside the record's transaction and raise `ActiveRecord::Rollback` when validation fails. When the email is actually blocked, the increment made during `save` is rolled back. Paths that only call `save!` (e.g. `User.create_for_email` for invites) never record blocked matches at all.

The result is that `match_count`/`last_match_at` are inconsistent and unreliable, which is the stated purpose of these columns. Don't write to the database from inside a validator; record the match explicitly after the create attempt, outside the user's transaction.

findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is an exact, case-sensitive match and is trivially bypassed
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` compares the raw submitted value. Neither the stored email nor the input is downcased or stripped. If `bad@spammers.org` is blocked, a spammer can register as `Bad@spammers.org` or `BAD@SPAMMERS.ORG` and pass validation. The uniqueness validation on `BlockedEmail.email` is also case-sensitive, so case-variant duplicates can be inserted. Normalize the email (e.g. `Email.downcase(email).strip`) both when storing and when looking up, or compare with `lower(email)`.

findings.title: match_count increment is a racy read-modify-write
findings.body: `should_block?` loads the record, does `record.match_count += 1`, and then calls `record.save`. Concurrent signup attempts for the same email can read the same value and overwrite each other's increment, losing counts. Each save also triggers a uniqueness-validation query. Use an atomic update instead, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`.

findings.title: Any server-side email error permanently marks the address as 'invalid' on the client
findings.body: The client pushes the email into `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` is present. That includes errors like "has already been taken" or the domain whitelist/blacklist message, not only the new blocked-email error. From then on, the inline validation for that address shows the generic `user.email.invalid` text, which is misleading for the "already taken" case. The address also stays rejected for the rest of the page session, because `rejectedEmails` is never cleared.

findings.title: No tests for the end-to-end blocking or the new create response fields
findings.body: The specs only exercise `EmailValidator#validate_each` with `should_block?` stubbed, and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in isolation. Nothing verifies that `User` actually rejects a blocked email through `valid?`/`save`. Nothing covers the new `errors`/`values` keys in the `UsersController#create` failure response that the JS now depends on, or the match-count behavior through the real controller flow. The double-count and rollback problems in `should_block?` would have been caught by such tests.
